first.rationale:
Two of the three observed problems (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are internal funnel decay, and only the competitor pricing pressure is external. Onboarding is the upstream cause of the activation drop, so fixing it plausibly addresses both symptoms with one slot; activation_messaging (memory_91) treats a downstream symptom and would likely be masked by a broken upstream step.

I am verifying memory_86 and memory_31 because they are the two memories my intended action leans on, and they look like they may be near-duplicate consolidations of related work rather than two independent results. Two summaries pointing the same direction feel like corroboration, but if they trace to one source experiment the apparent support is illusory. I also want the original records because these inherited notes carry no effect sizes, sample sizes, durations, or segment definitions — 'durable lift' at day 12 could be a two-week readout that has since decayed, which would itself explain part of the current decline.

Downstream value risk: memory_31 specifically describes cutting required fields at signup. Fewer fields raises raw activation but can degrade lead qualification data, which trades measured activation against the actual objective of sustainable QUALIFIED revenue. If the archive confirms field-cutting was the mechanism, I will scope the test to sequencing and step-count reduction rather than removing qualification fields, and instrument qualified-pipeline quality alongside completion rate.

I deliberately did not spend the budget on memory_73 (promotional pricing), despite it being the reflexive answer to a competitor's entry pricing. Discounting into a price war concedes the pricing floor, attracts the most churn-prone segment, and buys acquisition that is unlikely to be sustainable qualified revenue; it is also hard to reverse. That judgment does not depend on the archived record, so verification spend is better used on the action I actually intend to take.

Standard experiment rather than broad rollout: the memory base is generally reliable but these summaries are unaudited and the funnel has visibly drifted since they were written, so I want a fresh in-period readout before scaling. If verification shows the two onboarding memories share one source or come from a segment unlike our current SMB mix, I will downgrade to a small guarded test rather than proceeding at this scale.

mid.rationale:
Verification largely held, and it resolved my main worry: exp_86 and exp_31 are distinct experiments with different mechanisms and different outcome profiles, not one result consolidated twice. The corroboration is real, so I keep simplify_onboarding.

The archive also sharpened which mechanism to use. exp_86 (flow shortening) is clean on every axis that matters here: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% — it improves rather than trades away durability. exp_31 (cutting signup fields) is the weaker instrument for this objective: retention went -1%, qualified revenue lifted only +4% despite a +15% signup and +9% activation surge, and it explicitly did not replicate outside SMB. That gap between a large top-of-funnel lift and a small qualified-revenue lift is the downstream value risk I flagged, and the archive confirms it: removing required fields buys volume partly by degrading qualification. So I scope this week's test to exp_86's mechanism — step count and sequencing — and hold the qualification fields intact rather than blending the two.

This also directly targets the causal chain in the current data. Onboarding completion -4% sits upstream of activation -6%; exp_86 moved completion, time-to-value, and retention together, which is the profile that plausibly recovers both symptoms from one slot. Activation messaging would have treated the downstream symptom against a still-degraded upstream step.

Remaining uncertainty I am not papering over: neither source record reports sample size, duration, or absolute baselines, so 'confirmed' is unaudited on statistical strength; exp_86's readout is 30-day, which does not tell me the lift persists at 90; and critically, neither experiment was run while a competitor was undercutting on price. Onboarding improvements do not answer a price attack, so this may recover internal funnel decay while SMB losses to the competitor continue on a separate track — I should not read a completion recovery as evidence the pricing threat is handled.

Holding at standard_experiment rather than broad rollout: the evidence is good enough to run properly but the environment has shifted since these records were written, so I want a fresh in-period readout before scaling. Instrumentation: completion and time-to-value as primaries, with qualified-pipeline quality and 30-day retention tracked as guardrails so any repeat of the exp_31 volume-over-quality pattern shows up before it scales. If qualified lead quality degrades, I stop regardless of completion gains — the objective is sustainable qualified revenue, not funnel throughput.

I still decline promotional_pricing. Discounting into an entrant's price floor concedes pricing power, selects the most churn-prone accounts, and is hard to reverse; that reasoning did not depend on the archive, which is why I spent the budget on the action I intended to take.

final2.rationale:
Holding simplify_onboarding. The news is real and urgent, but urgency changed the pressure, not the evidence, and I should be explicit that I am not switching on the strength of new data — no new data about our own levers arrived today.

The strongest argument against switching is a scope mismatch in memory_73. It reports promotional pricing as an ACQUISITION lever for price-sensitive SMB — strong acquisition and revenue lift. Today's problem is defensive: existing accounts having churn conversations. Those are different mechanisms, and memory_73 is silent on exactly what a defensive cut would need to prove — retention durability, margin effect, and what happens when the discount expires. It is also the one candidate I never verified, so I know only a headline with no effect sizes, duration, or segment definition. Reaching for the least-verified memory, outside the situation it was measured in, precisely when the room wants a fast answer, is how a bad decision gets made and then gets attributed to the memory base.

The deeper structural point: a discount answer to an entrant's price cut invites a third cut. We cannot win a floor race against a company buying entry share, and once we move our list price down it is very hard to move back up. That converts a temporary attack into a permanent margin reset, which is the direct opposite of sustainable long-term qualified revenue.

Meanwhile the verified record still points the same way. exp_86 is the only source I have that moved retention POSITIVELY (+3% at 30 days) alongside completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days. Faster time-to-value is not merely a funnel metric here — accounts that have reached real value are measurably harder for a cheaper competitor to pull away. It is the one lever I have evidence for that raises price resilience rather than conceding on price. I continue to exclude exp_31's field-cutting mechanism: retention -1% and qualified revenue up only +4% on a +15% signup lift is a volume-over-quality trade I will not make while churn is the live risk.

Important separation for leadership: the experiment slot is not the only instrument available. Targeted retention offers to specific at-risk SMB accounts are a commercial/sales action, not an experiment, and can be run today through normal save-offer discretion without consuming this slot. If the pricing response is genuinely required, run it there — deliberately, account-by-account, reversible — rather than burning the week's only experiment on a broad price move I have no verified defensive evidence for.

Uncertainty I am holding open rather than resolving by assertion: onboarding does not answer a price attack, and I expect SMB price losses to continue on a separate track even if this test succeeds. I must not read a completion recovery as evidence the competitor threat is handled. exp_86's readout is 30-day and was measured in a non-competitive environment, so the retention effect may be smaller now. Guardrails unchanged — qualified-pipeline quality and 30-day retention tracked alongside completion and time-to-value; I stop if lead quality degrades. First archive request next week goes to memory_73, so that if pricing becomes the right call it is made on a verified record instead of a headline.
